title: Queen's Gambit Accepted
description: One of Levy's favorite openings, the "QGA" is an easy opening that leads to great positions for Black below master level. Simply capture White's c4 pawn and let the fun begin.

r1bqk2r/p1pn1ppp/5n2/1pbPp1B1/2p1P3/2N2N.text:
We should just develop knowing that 8.Nxb5 runs into 8...Bxf2+. 

8.Be2 Rb8 is a normal line where we get to keep the strong queenside pawns safe.

rn1q1rk1/pb3ppp/2p5/3Pp3/1bB1n3/N4N2/PP3.text:
We can simply develop and attack the pawn.

This position is -2. 

We are clearly winning. 

Qb3 does nothing because of ...a5.

rnbq1rk1/p1p2ppp/8/1N1Pp3/1bB1n3/5N2/PP3.text:
White develops their knight.

We'll attack the knight and the pawn. 

The d-pawn is also pinned.

rnbq1rk1/p1p2ppp/8/1N1Pp3/1bB1n3/P7/1P3P.text: White can kick our bishop away.

rnbq1rk1/p1p2ppp/8/1NbPp3/2B1n3/P7/1P3PP.text:
But it's very obvious that White's opening hasn't gone well. 

We have the edge: their king is on f1. 

We will play ...c6 and blast the position open.

rnbq1rk1/p1p2ppp/8/3Pp3/2B5/8/P2B1PPP/Q3.text: White cannot even take on e5 because of ...Re8.

rnbq1rk1/p4ppp/2p5/3Pp3/1bB1n3/2N2N2/PP3.text:
If the knight goes back, we can at the very minimum win a pawn. But the position is worse than that for White.

We'll take on c3 with the bishop.

rnbq1rk1/p4ppp/2p5/3Pp3/1bB1n3/N4N2/PP3P.text: White is forced to the bad a3-square.

rnbq1rk1/p4ppp/2p5/3Pp3/2B1n3/2P2N2/P4PP.text:
They recapture.

And we'll take on c3 with the knight, hitting both the queen and the d5-pawn.

rnbq1rk1/p4ppp/2p5/3Pp3/2B5/1Qn2N2/P4PPP.text:
Now Qb3 attacks our knight.

But we don't even have to move it away. 

We can take another pawn and attack the bishop by playing cxd5.

rnbq1rk1/p4ppp/8/4p3/2p5/2Q2N2/P4PPP/R1B.text:
And we take the bishop. 

White cannot even take on c4 because of ...Ba6. White is totally lost.

rnbqk2r/p1p2ppp/5n2/1N1Pp1B1/2p1P3/8/PP3.text:
White takes.

We'll take on e4 with check.

rnbqk2r/p1p2ppp/5n2/1NbPp1B1/2p1P3/8/PP3.text:
This capture falls into our trap.

Now we can capture on f2 with check and set up a fork.

rnbqk2r/p1p2ppp/5n2/1pbPp1B1/2p1P3/2N2N2.text: If normal development with 7.Nf3, we still have a great position thanks to the pawns on b5 and c4.

rnbqk2r/p1p2ppp/8/1N1Pp1B1/2p1n3/4K3/PP4.text:
This is a very bad move.

We'll take the bishop with check.

rnbqk2r/p1p2ppp/8/1N1Pp1n1/2p5/8/PP4PP/R.text: We take with our knight because we need the queen to keep an eye on c7.

rnbqk2r/p1p2ppp/8/1N1Pp3/1bB1n3/8/PP3PPP.text:
White loses castling rights.

In contrast, we'll castle and get our king into safety.

rnbqk2r/p1p2ppp/8/3Pp3/1bB1n3/2N5/PP3PPP.text:
This move gives up material. 

We are winning. We'll capture on c3 with the knight.

rnbqk2r/p1p2ppp/8/3Pp3/1bB5/2P5/P4PPP/R1.text:
White recaptures.

And we take. This is check. We're going to win an exchange.

rnbqk2r/p1p2ppp/8/3Pp3/2B5/2b5/P2B1PPP/R.text:
White blocks.

And we'll capture on a1.

rnbqkb1r/p1p2ppp/5n2/1N1Pp3/2p1P3/8/PP3P.text:
The most popular move is 6.Nxb5. 

White simply captures. I suspect many people don't even see they're losing e4.

This is good for us.  

Our active knight will combine with our bishop which is coming to b4 with check.

rnbqkb1r/p1p2ppp/5n2/1p1Pp1B1/2p1P3/2N5/.text:
White could also pin us.

Now we should develop our dark-squared bishop. c5 is an aggressive location, with an hidden idea.

rnbqkb1r/p1p2ppp/8/1N1Pp3/2B1n3/8/PP3PPP.text:
White captures on c4. 

They also develop the bishop. 

However, our edge is clear. Now Bb4+ is awkward for White to meet.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/5n2/3Pp3/2p1P3/2N5/PP3P.text:
Close to 90% of games lead us to this position, which is our main line.

We should inconvenience White by defending c4. 

They now have to decide whether to take on b5 or not. 

If they don't take, we defend c4. If they do take, they lose e4!

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
This is the Queen's Gambit.

There are more than 200 million games in the database of it.

We will accept the gambit.

One of our goals is simply to develop our pieces and let White waste time recapturing the c4-pawn.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/8/2pP4/2N5/PP2PPPP/R.text:
3.Nc3 is the most popular move under 2000 rating. There are more than 18 million games in the database. 

It isn't particularly good because it doesn't prevent our 3...e5 move and it doesn't get closer to taking on c4.

We'll go ahead and reply with ...e5!

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3Pp3/2p5/2N5/PP2PPPP/.text:
This popular advance can also be reached via 3.e4. 

4.d5 is played nearly 47% of times and has more than 850,000 games in the database.

We will develop and start putting pressure on the pawn.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
Welcome to the Queen's Gambit Accepted! 

This is a popular opening. The odd thing about this gambit is that people do not always expect the capture of the c4-pawn and declining is more common. This gives our approach the element of surprise.  

White starts with 1.d4, and we'll reply with ...d5.

rnb1k2r/1pp1qp2/p2b3p/3PB1p1/P1pQ4/2P5/5.text: We will win material, thanks to the pin.

rnb1k2r/1pp1qp2/p6p/3PB1p1/PbpQn3/2N5/1P.text:
White defends the bishop and attacks our knight.

In order to get rid of the attack, we trade on c3.

We are moving out of danger with a tempo.

rnb1k2r/1pp2pp1/p4q1p/2bPp3/P1p1P3/2N5/1.text:
But like I said, this bishop is powerful. 

If Nf3, I like the continuation of ...g5 to threaten ...g4. 

Developing moves like ...Bg4 and Nbd7 later also come to mind.

rnb1kb1r/1pp2pp1/p4q1p/3Pp3/P1p1P3/2N5/1.text: White connects their pawns and prepares to capture on c4.

rnbqk2r/1pp2p2/p4n1p/3Pp1p1/Pbp1P3/2N3B1.text:
The bishop goes to g3. 

Sure, it attacks e5 now, but taking on e4 has no drawbacks.

rnbqk2r/1pp2p2/p6p/3PB1p1/Pbp1n3/2N5/1P3.text:
It isn't a good idea for White to take on e5.

We can align our queen on the open e-file, pointing at their king.

rnbqk2r/1pp2pp1/p4n1p/3Pp3/Pbp1P2B/2N5/1.text:
Let's suppose White defends d5.

We can get rid of the pin. 

White can't do likewise on the queenside because their a-pawn is on a4.

rnbqk2r/2p2ppp/p4n2/2bPp1B1/Ppp1P3/8/NP3.text:
And we simply develop. 

We will play moves like ...Qd6, Bb7 and Nbd7, along with 0-0. 

We have better placed pieces than White.

rnbqkb1r/1pp2pp1/p4B1p/3Pp3/P1p5/2N5/1P2.text:
If White takes, we have the bishop pair and an active queen.

Now our dark-squared bishop will have plenty of room to wander.

rnbqkb1r/1pp2pp1/p4n1p/3Pp3/P1p4B/2N5/1P.text:
They can also choose to keep the pin. This doesn't help White because the bishop isn't relevant on the kingside.

We'll bring our bishop into the game. 

Our pin is more effective than White's! It is an absolute pin and it undermines one of the defenders of d5.

rnbqkb1r/1pp2ppp/p4n2/3Pp1B1/2p1P3/2N5/P.text:
Some players connect the pawns now. 

We'll connect ours by playing ...b5.

rnbqkb1r/1pp2ppp/p4n2/3Pp1B1/P1p5/2N5/1P.text:
A solid attempt is to prevent ...b5 with a4.

Since White is taking care of their queenside, we can bring our attention back to the bishop on g5 by playing ...h6.

rnbqkb1r/2p2ppp/p4n2/1p1Pp1B1/P1p1P3/2N5.text:
White tries to break our pawns apart.

But our queenside pawns are mobile and they can displace the knight to a worse square.

This is the main problem with allowing ...b5 on the board.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/5n2/3Pp1B1/2p5/2N5/PP2P.text:
White pins our knight.

This has occurred in less than 10% of the games in the database, but being such a natural move it could easily happen.

Since White has wasted some time, we'll prepare ...b5 to defend the c4-pawn.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
This is the Queen's Gambit.

There are more than 200 million games in the database of it.

We will accept the gambit.

One of our goals is simply to develop our pieces and let White waste time recapturing the c4-pawn.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/8/2pP4/2N5/PP2PPPP/R.text:
3.Nc3 is the most popular move under 2000 rating. There are more than 18 million games in the database. 

It isn't particularly good because it doesn't prevent our 3...e5 move and it doesn't get closer to taking on c4.

Therefore we'll push ...e5!

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3Pp3/2p5/2N5/PP2PPPP/.text:
This popular advance can also be reached via 3.e4. 

4.d5 is played nearly 47% of times and has more than 850,000 games in the database.

We'll develop and start putting pressure on the d-pawn.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
In this study, we'll continue our exploration of the Queen's Gambit Accepted with 3.Nc3.

For this second study, I simply want us to see how to play if White pins our knight earlier with 5.Bg5.

White starts with 1.d4, and we'll reply with ...d5.

3rr1k1/pppq1pp1/2nb1n1p/5b2/1PBP4/P1N1BN.text:
We centralize our connected rooks and get ready to have a stable middlegame. 

You cannot go wrong with moves like ...a6, and Re7 to double up on the e-file.

r1b2r1k/pppn2p1/2n1B2p/8/8/8/PP3PPP/R1BN.text:
And we place our king on h8. We have many plans depending on how White continues. 

All we have to do is keep in mind that we can often improve the d7-knight by moving it to b6, and a tactical ...Nd4 may be useful at some point.

If there are further trades we'll have a promising endgame with a queenside pawn majority.

r1b2rk1/ppp2pp1/1n5p/4P3/3n1P2/1B6/PP4PP.text:
And we jump the knight to d4 and attack the bishop.

We will take on b3 and have a promising endgame with control of the light squares, while also bringing a rook to d8.

r1b2rk1/ppp2pp1/2n2n1p/4P3/2B5/8/PP3PPP/.text:
White recaptures with the knight. The rook needs to keep an eye on e5.

But with our knight move to d7, we force White to address the issue of the potentially over-extended e-pawn.

r1b2rk1/pppn1pp1/2n1P2p/8/2B5/8/PP3PPP/R.text:
An option they have is to push it. 

But if we simply remain cool under this situation, we realize that we're fine after some trades.

We'll take on e6.

r1b2rk1/pppn1pp1/2n4p/4P3/2B2P2/8/PP4PP/.text:
White can choose to build a large center rather than push e6.

Our knights now gain some activity, though.

r1bq1rk1/ppp1npp1/3b1n1p/3P4/2B5/2N1BN2/.text: White develops, bringing out their last minor piece.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2pp1/2n2n1p/4P3/2B5/2N5/PP3P.text:
White recaptures. 

They get rid of the isolani.

We will trade queens because this minimizes White's play.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2pp1/2nb1n1p/3P4/2B5/2N2N2/P.text:
White can push the IQP. 

It isn't winning or anything, and it may in fact make the pawn weaker in the long-term.

We go back, and place some pressure on d5.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2pp1/2nb1n1p/4N3/2BP4/2N5/PP.text:
This move looks active, but it simply allows us to trade. 

Trading isn't what White wants.

We take with the bishop, opening up the option of a queen exchange.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2pp1/2nb1n1p/8/2BP4/2N1BN1P/.text:
The bishop goes to e3.

We can bring our bishop out to f5 where it's actively placed.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2pp1/2nb1n1p/8/2BP4/2N1BN2/P.text:
This move isn't at all concerning. White is blocking their e-file activity.

Now our bishop on f5 becomes very active. 

We can already be said to be equal, which doesn't speak highly of White's opening.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2pp1/2nb1n1p/8/2BP4/P1N2N2/1.text:
10.a3 seeks to push b4, and creates a square on a2 for the bishop.

However, we are giving White no time to play on the queenside. 

We pin the f3-knight. There's a very serious threat to take on f3 and then on d4. 

After 11.Be3, we have forced White to block their own rook and we occupy the e-file ourselves with ...Re8.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2pp1/3b1n1p/3P1n2/2B5/2N1BN2.text:
But now we simply put our knight on f5. 

White actually helped us get there with 10.d5. 

Our next moves are simple: we will take on e3 if allowed, and play ...a6 to keep our bishop on d6 stable, with ...Re8 to control the e-file.

r2q1rk1/1pp2pp1/p1nb1n1p/5b2/2BP4/P1N1BN.text:
And we do the same to prevent ...Nb5. 

We will connect rooks with ...Qd7 and bring both of them to the center.

r2q1rk1/ppp2pp1/2nb1n1p/5b2/2BP4/P1N1BN1.text:
White prevents Nb4 ideas, creates a square for their bishop and prepares b4 if they want it.

We'll develop our queen and connect our rooks.

r2q1rk1/ppp2pp1/2nb1n1p/8/2BP2b1/P1N2N1P.text:
Let's take this mistake as an example of what could happen.

We'll take on f3 to remove the defender.

r2q1rk1/ppp2pp1/2nb1n1p/8/2BP4/P1N2Q1P/1.text:
White recaptures.

Now we can grab the d-pawn! 

...Nc2 is also a threat.

r2q1rk1/ppp2pp1/3b1n1p/8/2Bn4/P1NQ3P/1P3.text:
This move defends both the queen and the c2-square.

But we have a little trick with the knight.

r3r1k1/pppq1pp1/2nb1n1p/5b2/1PBP4/P1N1BN.text:
White has nothing better to do than centralize. 

If 13.b5 Na5 and suddenly we challenging White's queenside with a knight that cannot be dislodged from a5.

r3r1k1/pppq1pp1/2nb1n1p/5b2/2BP4/P1N1BN1.text:
Once again, centralizing rooks and ...a6 are good moves. 

There isn't much White has here, and that plays to the side without the IQP.

Our goal is to trade some pieces and to attack the d-pawn in a simplified position.

r4rk1/pppq1pp1/2nb1n1p/5b2/1PBP4/P1N1BN1.text:
b4 is something we might see at some point. 

White gains space on the queenside, but they aren't really doing much with it.

We'll activate our king's rook. The fact that we control the center is slightly more important than their queenside expansion.

r4rk1/pppq1pp1/2nb1n1p/5b2/2BP4/P1N1BN1P.text: The middlegame could continue with something like 12.Re1.

rn1qr1k1/ppp2pp1/3b1n1p/6B1/3P2b1/2N2N2/.text:
We will play ...Nc6 and a6 to keep our bishop safe on d6. 

In the next chapter, we will see similar positions with Bxf6 and Bh4; in both, we can go for our ...Nc6 development with an equal position.

rn1qr1k1/ppp2ppp/3b1n2/6B1/3P2b1/2N2N2/P.text: You most likely will see White castle. White doesn't want us to capture on f3 and have to take back with the pawn due to the e2-bishop being pinned.

rnbq1rk1/ppp2pp1/3b1n1p/8/2BP4/2N2N1P/PP.text:
White could also prevent ...Bg4 right away. 

This changes things but only so slightly.

Our knight still comes to c6.

rnbq1rk1/ppp2pp1/3b1n1p/8/2BP4/2N2N2/PP3.text:
An active move, taking control of the e-file.

We should simply develop to an active square as well, where we fight for the e5-square.

rnbq1rk1/ppp2ppp/3b1n2/6B1/2BP4/2N2N2/PP.text:
It's possible that White may pin us here.

But since we have a rook check on the open e-file, the pin isn't so effective. 

Our rook now helps control e4.

rnbq1rk1/ppp2ppp/3b1n2/8/2BP4/2N2N2/PP3P.text:
White castles now.

If we can avoid Bg5, we should, hence we'll play h6. 

We will then examine a couple of moves. 

9.Be3 is popular but it's not ideal for White: it's not the definition of active play that's required when you play with the IQP.

rnbqk2r/ppp2ppp/3b1n2/8/2BP4/2N2N2/PP3PP.text:
White develops their other knight with the goal of castling, too.

And we castle kingside. 

Our rook is now ready to enter the game, and we'll develop with the intention of playing against the IQP.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/5n2/8/2BP4/2N5/PP3PPP/R.text:
White has an active bishop on c4. 

Despite this, the position is equal.

We'll simply develop and get ready to castle.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
Now c4 is the Queen's Gambit.

We'll accept.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/8/2pP4/2N5/PP2PPPP/R.text:
White develops the knight.

We'll play e5, challenging the center.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/4p3/2pP4/2N1P3/PP3PPP.text:
White defends d4 while opening up an attack on c4.

This move has occurred around 20% of times in the database, in nearly 350,000 games.

We'll just take on d4 and give White an isolated queen's pawn (IQP).

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/8/2pP4/2N5/PP3PPP/R1B.text:
White recaptures. 

They now have an isolated pawn. 

Note that 5.Qxd4 would still give White an IQP after a queen trade on d4. Trading pieces isn't what the side with the IQP wants, so that would be better for us.

We'll bring our knight out to f6, developing while White captures on c4. 

We will develop while White captures on c4.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
In this study, we will continue our exploration of 3.Nc3. 

In this line as in almost all of the Queen's Gambit Accepted Lines, there's e3. White wants to capture the c4-pawn, whilst keeping their center supported.

It's important to see how to attack this rather popular set of moves.

We'll begin with 1.d4 and our reply of 1...d5.

rnbqr1k1/ppp2ppp/3b1n2/6B1/3P4/2N2N2/PP2.text:
The bishop blocks and enters a self-pin.

We'll develop, bringing our bishop to an active location.

2kr1b1r/ppp3pp/4bn2/5P2/2pnP3/2N5/PPK3PP.text:
We have a check. 

We will follow this up with 11...Nxf5 no matter what. 

11.Kb1 Nxf5 and White cannot take our knight because of impending disaster on the f5-b1 diagonal.

2kr1bnr/ppp2ppp/2n1b3/4P3/2p1P3/2N2N2/PP.text:
The bishop blocks.

We'll develop our bishop to c5 and attack f2.

2kr1bnr/ppp2ppp/2n1b3/4P3/2p1PP2/2N5/PPK.text:
Most people simply move out of the way with the king. 

No one volunteers to go into a pin.

And now's time to undermine White's central pawns. 

f5 guarantees that we'll reduce White's central control one way or the other.

2kr1bnr/ppp3pp/2n1bP2/8/2p1PP2/2N5/PPK3P.text:
White takes en passant.

But we'll recapture and get another piece developed, increasing our initiative.

2kr2nr/ppp2ppp/2n1b3/2b1P3/2p1P3/2N2N2/P.text: The king moves out of the pin and also defends f2.

2kr3r/ppp1nppp/2n1b3/2b1P3/2p1P3/2N2N2/P.text:
But we can simply develop and get ready to attack e5 some more. 

White has moved the king twice in the opening. 

We have better coordination and are ahead in development.

2kr3r/ppp1nppp/2n1b3/4P3/2p5/P1P1PN2/5PP.text: We have an excellent position, as the pawn on e5 is going to fall.

r1b1k1nr/ppp2ppp/2n5/4P3/1bp2P2/2N5/PP2P.text:
White could of course defend with the f-pawn.

We can just attack, semi-gambit style, playing for activity rather than to win the pawn outright.

This is a good move to keep in mind.

r1b1k1nr/ppp2ppp/2n5/4P3/1bp5/2N2N2/PP2P.text:
White may develop normally, supporting e5.

But one of our main plans is to attack e5. We'll bring our other knight out, with the intention of placing it on g6.

r1b1k1nr/ppp3pp/2n2P2/8/1bp2P2/2N5/PP2P1.text: After White captures, we recapture and have a good game.

r1b1k2r/ppp1nppp/2n5/4P3/1bp5/2N1PN2/PP3.text:
White hits the c4-pawn. 

But in this variation, our light-squared bishop can come into play very nicely. Compare this to Queen's Gambit Declined positions, where the bishop is trapped behind its own pawns!

r1b1k2r/ppp3pp/2n2n2/8/1bp2P2/2N5/PP2P1P.text:
Our bishop will go to f5 and we will castle queenside. 

After e3 we could even defend c4 with Bd3.

r3k1nr/ppp2ppp/2n1b3/4P3/2p5/5N2/PP1KPPP.text:
We will also make it extra hard for White to regain the pawn.

We also have an incoming plan to attack e5: Ne7 to g6.

r3k2r/ppp1nppp/2n1b3/4P3/1bp5/P1N1PN2/1P.text:
If we are prompted to trade, we will.

We now split the pawns.

r3kbnr/ppp2ppp/2n1b3/4P3/2p1P3/2N2N2/PP3.text:
White can defend e5 with their knight. 

This is a very human move but it's flawed.

We'll castle with check.

r3kbnr/ppp2ppp/2n1b3/4P3/2p1PP2/2N5/PP4P.text:
This is the best attempt according to the engine.

We castle with check.

White's best move according to Stockfish is the weird self-pin 8.Bd2, but don't expect to see many players find that.

rn2kbnr/ppp2ppp/4b3/4P3/2p1P3/2N5/PP3PPP.text:
6.e4 opens up an attacker on c4.

But we'll continue to develop, with tempo.

We are going from equal to a slight advantage.

rnb1k1nr/ppp2ppp/8/4P3/1bp5/2N5/PP2PPPP/.text:

rnbq1rk1/pp2nppp/8/2p5/2BNP3/8/PP1Q1PPP/.text:
And we push c5. We are going to utilize our queenside pawn majority to gain space. 

Once again, we don't shy away from the queen trade.

rnbqk1nr/ppp2ppp/8/4p3/1b1PP3/2P2N2/P2N1.text:
The pawn recaptures.

We'll take on c3. 

We have a pin on the knight and an attack on the a1-rook.

rnbqk1nr/ppp2ppp/8/4p3/1bpPP3/5N2/PP1B1P.text:
This move happens about 35% of times. 

White wants a bishop trade.

We don't mind accepting the trade because it allows us to keep developing rapidly.

rnbqk1nr/ppp2ppp/8/4p3/1bpPP3/5N2/PP1N1P.text:
This is another way White can block, but it's the most unpopular way. 

White blocks their dark-squared bishop in.

We can attack the knight and eliminate our problem c4-pawn.

rnbqk1nr/ppp2ppp/8/4p3/2pPP3/5N2/PP1N1PP.text:
This knight recapture is played about 40% of the time in the database. 

It's rarer because we can take on d4, and we're temporarily up two pawns.

rnbqk1nr/ppp2ppp/8/4p3/2pPP3/5N2/PP1Q1PP.text:
The queen can recapture. 

This is the most common move because White keeps the option of Nc3.

We'll simply take on d4 and try to get the queen to move again.

rnbqk1nr/ppp2ppp/8/4p3/3PP3/2b2N2/P2N1PP.text:
The rook goes to b1.

We'll take on d4 now and our pawn is defended by our bishop on c3. 

The fact that White will have to fight to break this d4-Bc3 combo apart means we have the advantage already.

rnbqk1nr/ppp2ppp/8/4p3/Qb1PP3/2p2N2/PP1N.text:
This check is an attempt to introduce some confusion to the position.

We can simply defend the bishop and block the check. 

There's still an attack on d2 so White has to react.

rnbqk1nr/ppp2ppp/8/8/2BpP3/2b2N2/P2N1PPP.text:
They develop. 

White may try to simply add pressure to f7 and develop since it's tough to attack d4.

We'll develop and support d4 further.

rnbqk1nr/ppp2ppp/8/8/2BpP3/5N2/PP1N1PPP/.text:
White takes a pawn. Now we're only up a pawn, but the question remains: how will White go about taking on d4?

We can develop and support d4 a bit more with Nc6.

rnbqk1nr/ppp2ppp/8/8/2BpP3/5N2/PP1Q1PPP/.text:
White could simply ignore our d-pawn for now.

But we can support it with c5, and there's nothing wrong with this pawn duo.

rnbqk1nr/ppp2ppp/8/8/2pNP3/8/PP1Q1PPP/RN.text:
The knight takes on d4.

We want to develop our kingside quickly so we can castle. Bringing the knight to e7 also supports a later ...Nc6.

rnbqk1nr/ppp2ppp/8/8/2pQP3/5N2/PP3PPP/RN.text:
White's queen moves yet again to recapture.

At this point we don't mind the queen trade because we have great potential in the endgame. 

We will mobilize the queenside pawn majority.

rnbqk2r/ppp1nppp/8/8/2BNP3/8/PP1Q1PPP/RN.text:
White takes back on c4.

And we'll castle.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
The Queen's Gambit.

We'll accept it!

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/8/2pPP3/8/PP3PPP/RNB.text:
White places two pawns in the center.

We'll challenge White's pawn duo with e5.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/4p3/2BPP3/8/PP3PPP/RN.text:
Another option White has is to take on c4 right away. 

This isn't so popular and I think it's because it looks weird to lose d4.

We'll take and offer a queen exchange.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/4p3/2pPP3/5N2/PP3PPP/.text:
We shall resume our exploration of 4.Nf3, but with some less popular moves.

We will give a check like in the previous study.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
In this study, we'll be concluding our examination of 3.e4 and 4.Nf3, plus considering another fourth move option for White.

Let's begin! White opens with 1.d4, and we'll reply symmetrically with 1...d5.

r1b2rk1/ppp2pp1/2nb1q1p/8/2BPN3/5N2/PP3P.text:
White centralizes the knight and wants to eliminate our bishop pair.

Our queen is nicely placed on f4 and supports the bishop.

r1b2rk1/ppp2pp1/2nq3p/8/2BP4/5N2/PP3PPP/.text:
And we'll recapture with our queen to keep the pawn structure intact. 

We can target the isolated d4-pawn with ...Rd8 as well as ...Bg4.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2p2/2n2n1p/6p1/2BP4/5NPP/PP4.text:
White recaptures. 

Now their pawns are doubled in front of their king.

We'll push further, intending to damage their structure even more!

r1bq1rk1/ppp2p2/2nb1n1p/6p1/2BP4/5NBP/PP.text:
White retreats the bishop.

We'll capture and damage White's pawn structure.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2pp1/2nb1n1p/8/2BP3B/2N2N2/P.text:
White develops their queenside knight as well, which happens in 70% of the games.

In Chapter 2, we played ...h6 as early as possible. Now we didn't get the opportunity, so White was able to accomplish Bg5. 

Now, by pinning the knight we indirectly attack the pawn on d4 by threatening to trade on f3.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2pp1/2nb1n1p/8/2BP3B/5N1P/PP.text:
This is the strongest move-order, happening in around 10% of the games.

We'll play g5 and kick the bishop away from h4, getting rid of the pin on our knight.

r2q1rk1/pQp2pp1/3b1B1p/5n2/2B5/2N4P/PP3P.text: ...so they decide to trade it off for our knight.

r2q1rk1/pQp2pp1/3b1n1p/8/2Bn3B/2N4P/PP3P.text:
White captures on b7 to keep material equality.

We'll attack the bishop on h4 now.

The bishop doesn't have many good squares to go to...

r2q1rk1/ppp2p2/2B4p/6p1/3P2b1/5N2/PP3PPK.text:
White captures...

We'll check with the queen on d6.

r2q1rk1/ppp2p2/2B4p/6p1/3P2b1/5Nb1/PP3PP.text:
White must trade on c6 not to lose a piece.

And here comes a desperado move! 

White must capture since it comes with a check.

r2q1rk1/ppp2p2/2n2n1p/8/2BP2b1/5NP1/PP4P.text:
And we recapture with a pin on the knight! 

With moves like ...Qd6, ...Rd8 we'll add pressure to the d4-square.

...Kg7 could be a move to add safety to our king.

r2q1rk1/ppp2p2/2n4p/3Q2p1/2B5/6PP/PP4P1/.text:
White recaptures.

We'll trade the queens as well. Our king will feel much safer.

r2q1rk1/ppp2p2/2nb1N1p/6p1/2BP2bB/5N2/PP.text:
White trades the knights.

We'll recapture with the queen.

r2q1rk1/ppp2p2/2nb1n1p/3N2p1/2B5/3Q2BP/P.text:
White retreats.

We'll get rid of the dangerous knight.

r2q1rk1/ppp2p2/2nb1n1p/3N2p1/2BP2b1/5NB1.text:
Instead of capturing, White retreats the bishop.

We'll trade off the dangerous d5-knight.

r2q1rk1/ppp2p2/2nb3p/3B2p1/3P2b1/5NB1/PP.text:
White recaptures.

By trading on g3 we unleash an attack on the d5-bishop.

r2q1rk1/ppp2p2/2nb3p/3Q2p1/2B5/6BP/PP3PP.text:
White recaptures.

We'll trade to damage the pawn structure once again.

r2q1rk1/ppp2pp1/2nb1n1p/3N4/2B4B/3Q3P/PP.text:
White adds pressure to the knight on f6.

We'll free our knight by breaking the pin.

r2q1rk1/ppp2pp1/2nb1n1p/3N4/2BP2bB/5N2/P.text:
White immediately adds pressure to the f6-knight by jumping to d5.

We'll break the pin by pushing ...g5.

r2q1rk1/ppp2pp1/2nb1n1p/8/2BP2bB/2N2N1P/.text:
White can't stop us taking on f3. They attack our bishop.

As planned, we capture on f3.

r2q1rk1/ppp2pp1/2nb1n1p/8/2BP3B/2N2Q1P/P.text:
White recaptures with their queen in order not to damage their pawn structure.

We'll grab the d-pawn with tempo!

r2q1rk1/ppp2pp1/3b1n1p/8/2Bn3B/2NQ3P/PP3.text:
White brings the queeen to d3.

We'll retreat the knight, aiming to jump to the e5-square.

r4r2/ppp2pk1/2n4p/3B2p1/8/6PP/PP4P1/R4RK.text: And with ...Kg7 we get out of the bishop's eye and play this endgame with a pawn up and more space on the kingside.

r4rk1/pQp2pp1/3b1q1p/5n2/2B5/2N4P/PP3PP1.text:
And we recapture with the queen.

This position is equal, but we could argue that our pieces have better coordination.

Our play should revolve around the semi-open b-file, which our rook will occupy and try to do some damage.

r4rk1/ppp2p2/2nb1q1p/6p1/2BP2b1/5NB1/PP3.text:
White retreats the bishop.

We'll trade on f3, weakening the pawn on d4.

r4rk1/ppp2p2/2nb1q1p/6p1/2BP4/5QB1/PP3PP.text:
White recaptures with the queen.

We'll trade, further weakening the pawn structure.

r4rk1/ppp2p2/2q4p/6p1/3P2b1/5N2/PP3PP1/R.text:
...and this was the point of giving a check on d6. We can recapture on c6 with a queen and keep our structure intact. 

The d4-pawn is yet again a target, and we are also a pawn up.

r4rk1/ppp2p2/3b3p/6p1/2Bn4/5PB1/PP3P1P/R.text: And we win a clean pawn with an additional attack on another one!

rnb2rk1/ppp2pp1/3b1q1p/8/2BP4/2N2N2/PP3P.text:
White develops their knight to c3.

Our development revolves around the isolated d4-pawn. 

By bringing the knight to c6 we'll put some pressure on it.

rnbq1rk1/ppp2pp1/3b1B1p/8/2BP4/5N2/PP3PP.text:
White decides to not move the bishop anywhere and trades for our knight on f6.

We'll recapture with the queen.

rnbq1rk1/ppp2pp1/3b1n1p/8/2BP3B/5N2/PP3P.text:
9 out of 10 times White decides to retreat to h4 here and keep the pin.

We'll develop our knight to c6 where it eyes the isolated d-pawn.

rnbq1rk1/ppp2ppp/3b1n2/6B1/2BP4/5N2/PP3P.text:
White pins the knight to our queen.

We'll play h6, a standard move to ask the bishop on g5 a question.

rnbqk1nr/ppp2ppp/3b4/8/2BP4/5N2/PP3PPP/R.text:
More than half the games continue like this.

6.Nc3 occurs in 20% of the games but has no independent value and will most likely transpose.

We should develop. We are one step away from castling.

rnbqk2r/ppp2ppp/3b1n2/8/2BP4/5N2/PP3PPP/.text:
White hides their king.

7.Nc3 0-0 transposes to Chapter 1.

We get our king out of the center as well.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
The Queen's Gambit!

We'll accept it.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/8/2pP4/4P3/PP3PPP/RN.text:
This move occurs in about 27% of the games in the database. 

The idea is simple: defend d4 and take on c4.

We'll go for the same pawn break we've been playing. 

The point is to undermine the pawn chain and to create an isolated queen's pawn.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/4p3/2BP4/4P3/PP3PPP/R.text:
White takes. This is the most popular move, appearing in 80% of games in the database.

We now continue and trade to give White the isolani.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/8/2BP4/8/PP3PPP/RNBQK.text:
5.Qxd4 is bad because it would still result in trades and the IQP. 

Instead, White recaptures with the pawn and resolves to keep the queens on.

We'll develop our dark-squared bishop to its most active square.

Another important factor is we start fighting for e5 control. White likes playing moves like Ne5 in these IQP positions.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
In this study, we'll analyze 3.e3 - White defends their d4-pawn and opens up an attack on the c4-pawn. 

It's a conservative approach, which allows us to take the game in the direction we want.

Let's begin, with White playing 1.d4 and us replying symmetrically with 1...d5.

1rb1kb1r/1pp2ppp/p1n5/3NP3/P1p1P1n1/4BN2.text:
If they defend f2 with the bishop...

We'll capture it!

1rb1kb1r/1pp2ppp/p1n5/4P3/P1p1P3/4NN2/1P.text:
The knight recaptures so that White avoids the tripled pawns.

It seems like they've defended against all the threats and are looking to finally capture on c4.

1rb1kb1r/2p2ppp/p1n5/1p2P3/P1p1P3/4NN2/1.text:
But we've actually got ...b5, the hidden point of Rb8! We couldn't play b5 with the rook on a8, because White could play axb5 when our a-pawn would be pinned.

Whenever you are allowed to play b5 in these positions, you should.

Next, we will develop with ...Bc5 and castle.

r1b1k2r/1pp2ppp/p2b4/4B3/P1p1P3/2N5/1P3P.text:
White can capture, but the disadvantage of that is giving up the bishop pair.

And we'll get a monster bishop in the center.

r1b1k2r/1pp2ppp/p7/3PN3/P1p1P2q/1nP5/4K1.text:
It doesn't matter much what White plays here...

As we will capture on e4 with check either way, and fork the knight and the rook as well.

r1b1k2r/1pp2ppp/p7/3PN3/P1p1q3/1nP1B3/4K.text: White blocks and protects the rook...

r1b1k2r/1pp2ppp/p7/3Pq3/P1p5/1nP1B3/4K1P.text:
But we capture a free piece.

In the end, we are up two pawns and White's king is out in the open, blocking its own pieces.

A move like ...Bg4 is the immediate threat and White won't be able to escape.

We are completely winning.

r1b1kb1r/1pp2ppp/p1n2n2/4P3/P1p1P3/2N2N2.text:
They will probably take with the king, which actually works in our favor.

We have a fork now, which was our plan from the start.

With Ng4, we attack both the center and threaten another fork on f2 if White isn't careful.

r1b1kb1r/1pp2ppp/p1n5/3NP3/P1p1P1n1/5N2/.text:
Another move you could face, although I assume not very often, is Nd5.

Instead of defending against the fork, White threatens a fork of their own.

We would rather keep our threats active, so we will move the rook.

White mustn't capture on c7 now because of ...Kd8.

r1b1kb1r/1pp2ppp/p1n5/4N3/P1p1P3/2N5/1P3.text:
White trades...

And we'll recapture, conveniently defending the c4-pawn.

However, White has a continuation that eventually wins back the pawn.

If you know your stuff, this shouldn't bother much, though.

r1b1kb1r/1pp2ppp/p1n5/4P3/P1p1P1n1/2N1BN.text:
White might think that we will lazily capture on e5 if they protect the f2-pawn with the bishop.

But we've got something better.

We will actually take the bishop instead!

r1b1kb1r/1pp2ppp/p1n5/4P3/P1p1P1n1/2N2N2.text:
A simple defensive move White can make is Ke1, defending against the fork.

But that only takes care of one of the threats.

We can go ahead and capture on e5, executing the other threat.

r1b1kb1r/1pp2ppp/p1n5/4P3/P1p1P3/2N1PN2/.text:
White recaptures, and now they have tripled pawns on the e-file.

Horrible to look at, but pleasant to play against.

r1b1kb1r/1pp2ppp/p7/4n3/P1p1PB2/2N5/1P3P.text:
Because even if they take on c4, we'll still have a good position as you will soon see.

First of all, White goes after our defender, as one should.

I suggest we just protect it with the bishop.

r1bq1rk1/1pp2ppp/p4n2/3PN3/PbB1P3/2N2P2/.text:
So do we, and the advantage is on our side.

We probably won't be able to save the knight, but we have the material advantage either way.

We should chip away at the center with ...c6, as well as improve and attack the knight with ...Re8 next.

r1bqk2r/1pp2ppp/p4n2/3PN3/PbB1P3/1nN2P2/.text:
White can realize what's going on and choose to give up the rook.

This is actually the best move, which only signifies how strong our position is.

We'll take on a1.

r1bqk2r/1pp2ppp/p4n2/3PN3/Pbp1P3/1nN2P2/.text:
A move that seems logical is to simply move the rook.

But it's a big mistake that loses the game on the spot.

Can you spot a tactic now that takes advantage of White's f3?

We can sacrifice the knight on e4!

White can't defend with Bd2 because of the knight on b3, which is why ...Nb3 first is important.

r1bqk2r/1pp2ppp/p4n2/n2P4/PbN1P3/2N5/1P3.text:
White can choose to make this trade on c4.

But we will simply take in the center, now threatening to capture on c3.

r1bqk2r/1pp2ppp/p4n2/n2PN3/Pbp1P3/2N2P2/.text:
Another move that White can play, thinking it's natural, is f3.

But it is a big mistake.

Our idea wasn't only to attack the knight on c3.

Firstly, let's attack the rook on a1.

r1bqk2r/1pp2ppp/p7/3PN3/P1p1P3/1nP5/6PP/.text:
White recaptures.

And now the check on h4 is deadly, because it forks the king and the e4-pawn.

r1bqk2r/1pp2ppp/p7/3PN3/Pbp1P3/1nN5/1P4P.text:
So, they accept the sacrifice.

But now the h4-e1 diagonal is open.

First, we will remove the knight. It is defending the e4-pawn.

r1bqk2r/1pp2ppp/p7/N2P4/Pb2n3/2N5/1P3PPP.text: If White takes on a5, don't rush capturing on c3.

r1bqk2r/1pp2ppp/p7/b2P4/P3n3/2N5/1P3PPP/.text:
Simply recapture on a5 first.

White still has to deal with the pinned knight and now their center isn't as strong anymore.

We've got the advantage.

r1bqkb1r/1pp1pppp/p1n2n2/8/P1pPP3/2N2N2/.text:
A move you will face a lot and the one you probably have to be most prepared for is e4.

White grabs space in the center and those pawns already look dangerous.

Let's play a surprising move and sacrifice a pawn with e5! 

This move gives us space, prevents e5 and attacks White's center.

r1bqkb1r/1pp2pp1/p4n1p/n2Pp3/P1p1P2B/2N2.text: White retreats, and all they've done  is give us a tempo to continue with an important move.

r1bqkb1r/1pp2ppp/p1n2n2/3Pp3/P1p1P3/2N2N.text:
A logical move is White pushing d5.

This doesn't mean that they are rejecting the sacrifice but that they want to capture on e5 in another way.

The point is to remove our knight from c6 and capture in the center. We'll protect the c4-pawn.

r1bqkb1r/1pp2ppp/p1n2n2/4P3/P1p1P3/2N2N2.text:
White can get "insulted" by our last move and capture, not believing in any potential compensation for our side.

I suggest we trade queens here.

This will either force White to lose castling rights or make them give up the e4-pawn.

r1bqkb1r/1pp2ppp/p4n2/n2PN3/P1p1P3/2N5/1.text:
It might seem like White has the upper hand, having regained material equality and attacking the c4-pawn twice.

But we're not done complicating things.

And this time we will do that with ...Bb4.

White can go after c4, but we will go after e4!

r1bqkb1r/1pp2ppp/p4n2/n2Pp1B1/P1p1P3/2N2.text:
Another move they can play is Bg5.

In this position, there isn't much to worry about, though, thanks to our ...e5 idea.

Let's attack that bishop and push it back.

r2qkb1r/1pp2pp1/p4n1p/n2Pp3/P1p1P1bB/2N2.text:
We pin their knight on f3.

Now they won't even be able to capture on e5.

If they attack you with h3, simply capture on f3 and we maintain an advantage. White still hasn't won back the pawn on c4.

r3k2r/1ppb1ppp/p7/4b3/P1B1P3/2N5/1P3PPP/.text:
And we will develop to d7, preparing castling.

Castling queenside is more active here because we will immediately have a rook on the d-file.

Don't forget to play ...f6 first and avoid hanging your f7-pawn.

Black is better because of the bishop pair and activity to come.

r3kb1r/1pp2ppp/p1n1b3/4P3/P1p1P3/2N1PN2/.text:
First, we will defend our pawn, of course. Don't forget that.

Next, we will slowly develop and target those weak pawns.

rnbqkb1r/1pp1pppp/p4n2/8/P1pP4/2N2N2/1P2.text:
Studies 1 and 2 will cover 5.a4, the most popular way to deal with our plan.

About 35% of games see the move 5.a4 played. This is nearly 80,000 games! 

It's the most logical move that grabs space and controls the b5-square.

We'll play Nc6 and exert pressure on the white center.
We'll develop with ...Nc6, aiming firstly at central control, but with the option of going to a5 to protect the pawn if needed.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/8/2pP4/2N2N2/PP2PP.text:
And White goes for 4.Nc3, reinforcing the e4-square and potentially preparing to play e4.

This is the most common move here, played 43% of the time.

However, White hasn't moved the e-pawn yet and thus hasn't attacked our c4-pawn.

Therefore a good idea would be to prepare ...b5 and set up a light-squared pawn structure on the queenside.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
The Queen's Gambit is on the board.

And we'll accept the gambit.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/8/2pP4/5N2/PP2PPPP/R.text:
White now jumps to f3 and controls the e5-square.

This move is played 9% of the time.

Since we can't play e5, I suggest we instead develop the knight to f6.

White has given us time to take control of the e4-square.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
So far, one of our main points of attack in the early stage was advancing the e-pawn to ...e5.

But what if White purposely decides to play Nf3 on move 3, thus avoiding ...e5?

This is what Chapter 4 will analyze. Let's begin, starting with 1.d4 d5.

r1bqkb1r/1pp1pp1p/p4np1/n3N1B1/P1pP4/2N1.text:
Expect White harassing that c4-pawn as much as they can in the opening.

However, our setup is designed so that we have enough defensive resources.

r1bqkb1r/1pp1pppp/p1n2n2/6B1/P1pP4/2N2N2.text:
Another move they can play is Bg5, attacking our knight on f6.

The idea is that we can't easily play ...e6 now. e4 and possibly e5 would then be dangerous, owing to the pin on the knight.

This move occurs 13% of the time.

I recommend moving forward with our plan and defending the c4-pawn with Na5, when the b3-square could serve later on as a great outpost for our knight.

That is the downside of playing a4.

r1bqkb1r/1pp1pppp/p1n2n2/8/P1pP4/2N1PN2/.text:
6.e3 is the more passive version of 6.e4, which we saw previously. 

White attacks c4 but preserves the pawn chain.

About 30% of the games in the database go like this.

As mentioned, the most logical defense is ...Na5.

r1bqkb1r/1pp1pppp/p4n2/n3N3/P1pP4/2N1P3/.text:
If White piles up on the pawn, there's only one move to defend.

And we will play it with Be6.

Our bishop is not the strongest piece in the world, but remember that we are up a pawn.

If we can keep that c4-pawn while activating our pieces in the best way possible, White will have little to no compensation for it.

r1bqkb1r/1pp1pppp/p4n2/n5B1/P1pP4/2N1PN2.text:
White choosing e3 is the calmer approach.

It still attacks our pawn but doesn't grab enough central space.

Since ...e6 might not be the best plan as mentioned, try to think of another way to develop the dark-squared bishop.

A simple approach is ...g6 with the idea of implementing a fianchetto.

We want to quickly finish kingside development and castle.

r1bqkb1r/1pp1pppp/p4n2/n5B1/P1pPP3/2N2N2.text:
A more confrontational approach is e4 instead of e3.

White grabs much needed space and attacks the c4-pawn at the same time.

A good idea for them now would be to continue with Ne5 and add an attacker to the pawn, which would then be tough to defend.

That's why ...Bg4 is logical, pinning that knight and stopping Ne5.

r2q1rk1/1p2ppb1/p1p4p/3nP1p1/P1pP4/RnN2B.text:
And we can simply castle here.

White capturing on d5 would only undouble our pawns and protect c4.

Strengthening the knight further with ...e6 is a good idea. 

Depending on what White plays, we have different queenside plans, like maneuvering the knight to b4 and potentially playing ...a5.

...Nc7 could also be an idea to attack d4.

r2qk2r/1p2ppb1/p1p2n1p/4P1p1/P1pP4/1nN2B.text:
White can still try e5.

But we've got a nice outpost in the center, supported by the pawn. We'll play Nd5.

This is why it was so important to play ...c6 instead of rushing with ...Nb3 on move 9.

Sure, we won't be able to take on d4 now, but our position is stable and solid.

r2qk2r/1p2ppb1/p1p2n1p/n5p1/P1pPP1b1/2N2.text:
Expect White to attack your bishop at any point.

There isn't much merit to retreating here, as capturing the knight actually provides some value, thus we'll take on f3.

This can also be seen in the 9.Bxf6 line.

r2qk2r/1p2ppb1/p1p2n1p/n5p1/P1pPP3/2N2BB.text:
The bishop recaptures, and we have a fork now.

We can attack both the rook and the d4-pawn.

If our pawn wasn't on c6 now, White would have a strong counter-attack: e5.

Now it isn't as potent.

r2qk2r/1p2ppb1/p1p4p/3nP1p1/P1pP4/RnN2BB.text: White has to move the rook...

r2qkb1r/1p2pp2/p1p2n1p/n5p1/P1pPP1b1/2N2.text:
White retreats to g3...

And our last move gave us time to develop the bishop.

Castling is certainly a move we want to play soon.

r2qkb1r/1p2ppp1/p1p2n1p/n7/P1pPP1bB/2N2N.text:
White castles first.

We still have to figure out how to activate the rest of our kingside.

I recommend an aggressive approach here.

We've got enough of a clamp on White's possible central advances that we can afford to weaken the king a bit.

r2qkb1r/1p2pppp/p3bn2/n1P1N3/P1p5/2N1P3/.text:
White captures and offers a queen trade.

But there is a much better move than trading.

r2qkb1r/1pp1pp1p/p3bnp1/n3N1B1/P1pP4/2N1.text:
Here is another reason we didn't play ...e6.

Now we can use that square for the bishop to keep the pawn defended.

r2qkb1r/1pp1ppp1/p4B1p/n7/P1pPP1b1/2N2N2.text:
We don't mind them capturing on f6.

Even though we get doubled pawns, the f6-pawn does a great job of restricting any e5-ideas by White.

r2qkb1r/1pp1ppp1/p4n1p/n7/P1pPP1bB/2N2N2.text:
White retreating to h4 keeps some tension on the knight.

We shouldn't rush with ...Nb3 here because there are still e5-ideas that could complicate matters.

We'll calmly play ...c6 instead.

The purpose of this move is to provide more control over d5.

That way, if e5 ever happens, we can easily jump to d5.

r2qkb1r/1pp1pppp/p3bn2/n3N3/P1pP4/2N1P3/.text:
If they want to continue in a passive manner they can develop the bishop to e2.

If White gives us enough room, we should look to be as active as possible.

And in this case ...c5 does the job!

White hasn't given us any problems to solve with e4, so why not undermine their pawn chain?

r2qkb1r/1pp1pppp/p3bn2/n3N3/P1pPP3/2N5/1.text:
White can choose to play e4 now, but why not just play e4 in the first place then?

Their knight on e5 is still a problematic piece, though.

Since White basically lost one tempo, we have enough time to offer a trade with Nd7.

We would love to remove that strong knight.

r2qkb1r/1pp1pppp/p4n2/n5B1/P1pPP1b1/2N2N.text:
White unpins.

Still, the Ne5 threat isn't as potent anymore because we could trade light-squared bishops in that case.

Let's go after their other trouble-maker, and harass the bishop with h6.

r2qkb1r/1pp2pp1/p4p1p/8/P1pPP1b1/1nN2N2/.text:
And that is to jump to b3, attacking the rook and the d4-pawn at the same time.

If White moves the rook, we will be able to capture the knight on f3 and eventually win the central pawn.

Black is much better here, if not outright winning.

r2qkb1r/1pp2pp1/p4p1p/n7/P1pPP1b1/2N2N2/.text:
White castling here is definitely a mistake that gives us the upper hand.

And our next move is actually something we've been aiming for from the start.

r2qkb1r/1ppNpppp/p3b3/n7/P1pPP3/2N5/1P3P.text: And White doesn't have many better options than trading.

r2qkb1r/1ppbpppp/p7/n7/P1pPP3/2N5/1P3PPP.text:
We'll recapture with the bishop, and we got what we wanted from the position.

It's not easy for White to attack the c4-pawn again.

Meanwhile, we will continue development with ...e6, which is now safe to play, and expand with ...b5.

r3kb1r/1pq1pppp/p3bn2/n1P1N3/P1p5/2N1P3/.text: We play this nicely timed fork and now have many plans. We can take the pawn on c5, put a rook on d8, play g6-Bg7-0-0, and sometimes even Nb3. Black is doing great.

rnbqkb1r/1pp1pppp/p4n2/8/P1pP4/2N2N2/1P2.text:
White prevents ...b5!

We aren't giving up on the c4-pawn yet, however.

...Nc6 is a developing move designed to first attack the center, and then rotate to a5 to protect the pawn if needed.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/8/2pP4/2N2N2/PP2PP.text:
And White goes for 4.Nc3.

This is one of the ways White can reinforce the e4-square and prepare to play a future e4.

White hasn't moved the e-pawn yet and therefore hasn't attacked our c4-pawn in any way.

...b5 is a good move if allowed by White, thus we'll play the preparatory a6.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
The Queen's Gambit is on the board.

We'll accept the gambit.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/8/2pP4/5N2/PP2PPPP/R.text:
White now jumps to f3 and controls the e5-square.

Since we can't play e5, we'll continue with natural development and play Nf6, taking control of the e4 square.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
For this second study, I wanted to show more moves that are possible after our main 5.a4. 

I'm talking about 6.e3 and 6.Bg5. 6.e3 is passive and 6.Bg5 seeks to undermine our knight and thus our central control.

Let's get started with 1.d4 and our symmetrical reply of 1...d5.

1n1q1rk1/2p2ppp/bn2p3/4P3/1bpP4/2N2N2/1P.text:
White does the same.

We did lose the pawn chain on the queenside, but White's pieces are passive and blocking each other.

1n1qk2r/2p2ppp/bn2p3/4P3/1bpP4/2N2N2/1P1.text:
White can't do much but develop...

In which case we'll castle.

1nb1k2Q/2p2p1p/1n2p3/1p2P3/2pP4/2P2N2/5P.text:
Once White takes, do not play ...Ke7 and allow Qf6+.

That would lose the game as White would be able to defend the bishop afterwards.

We have to play ...Kd7 so that there are no immediate checks.

White can't waste a move on bringing the queen back...

1nb4Q/2pk1p1p/1n2p3/1p2P3/2pP4/2P2N2/5PP.text: So they have to bring the king closer to the bishop.

1nb4Q/2pk1p1p/1n2p3/1p2P3/q1pP4/2P2N2/5P.text:
In which case we have ...Qa4+, checking White on the light-squared diagonal.

White has to stay on either the first or the second rank.

If they play Kd2, you have ...Qa2+. 

Otherwise we just go back to a1, and it's a draw by repetition.

1nbqk2r/2p2ppp/Rn2p3/4P3/1bpP4/2N2N2/1P1.text:
White trades.

And we'll take with the bishop.

Now we have two pieces protecting the c4-pawn.

3q1rk1/2p2ppp/bnn1p3/4P3/1bpP4/2N2N2/1P1.text:
Now we can develop naturally and target the d4-pawn.

The position is in the balance, but we are the ones with a clear target.

Rnb1k2r/2p2ppp/1n2p3/1p1qP3/1bpP2Q1/2N2N.text:
White captures our rook.

We'll take back.

qnb1k2r/2p2pQp/1n2p3/1p2P3/1bpP4/2N2N2/1.text:
And give up the g7-pawn.

Why did we play like this?

Well, we actually have a forced draw that starts by capturing the knight on c3.

qnb1k2r/2p2pQp/1n2p3/1p2P3/2pP4/2P2N2/5P.text:
Once White recaptures, the point is that their queen is too far away to defend their king.

So we will sacrifice the rook!

White can't defend the bishop easily.

rn1q1rk1/1bp1bppp/p3p3/1p1nN1B1/2pP4/2N1.text:
But we won't let them do that yet.

We would rather trade dark-squared bishops and relieve the tension that way.

White has nothing to show for being down a pawn and having to deal with our insanely strong queenside structure.

rn1q1rk1/1bp1bppp/p3pn2/1p2N1B1/2pP4/2N1.text:
White brings the bishop to f3.

They plan to trade off our strong bishop.

rn1qk2r/1bp1bppp/p3pn2/1p2N1B1/2pP4/2N1P.text:
An active move you will most likely face is Ne5, however.

That knight is strong in the center but don't be afraid of it.

The one thing we should count on is White offering a trade of bishops.

We can simply castle for the moment.

rn1qkb1r/1b2pppp/p1p2n2/1P4B1/2pP4/2N1PN.text:
But White will most likely capture on b5 anyway.

It's good for them to have an open a-file.

Of course, we will recapture with the c-pawn and maintain the pawn chain.

White's main course of action is to undermine it.

rn1qkb1r/1b2pppp/p4n2/1p4B1/2pP4/1PN1PN2.text:
Which they can do with b3 here.

We mustn't let them capture.

We will take on b3 instead.

It does break our pawns apart, but we still have a lot of space on the queenside.

rn1qkb1r/1b3ppp/p3pn2/1p4B1/3P4/1QN1PN2/.text:
And I suggest ...e6 here.

It controls the d5-square further and prepares to develop the dark-squared bishop.

Our knight is pinned for the moment but White has no real way of attacking it.

We'll finish development and castle next.

rn1qkb1r/1bp1pppp/p4n2/1p2P1B1/2pP4/2N2N.text:
You will most likely face e5 here, attacking the knight.

Let's escape to the center.

The d5-square is most comfortable.

rn1qkb1r/1bp1pppp/p4n2/1p4B1/2pP4/2N1PN2.text:
White continues with Be2, preparing castling.

The bishop doesn't have many squares to operate on.

When we've already developed the bishop to b7, going for ...e6 is a good idea.

It does leave our knight pinned but takes control of the key d5-square and prepares ...Be7.

rn1qkb1r/1bp1pppp/p4n2/1p4B1/P1pP4/2N1PN.text:
You should be prepared to face a4 at any point.

However, it's easier to deal with it once you've already played ...b5.

A simple defense is ...c6.

It does block the bishop for now...

rn1qkb1r/1bp1pppp/p7/1p1nP1B1/2pP4/2N2N2.text: White gets the bishop out, preparing castling...

rn1qkb1r/1bp2ppp/p3pn2/1p4B1/2pP4/2N1PN2.text:
White castles...

And we develop and unpin.

We got everything we wanted from the position.

We just need to develop the rest of the pieces and castle.

rn2k2r/1bp1bppp/p3p3/1p1qP3/3P4/1P3N2/4B.text:
And we prepare castling.

As mentioned, White gave us all the freedom in the world in this line.

We got our strong queenside structure, developed our pieces optimally and will have a safe king.

On top of that, we are still up a pawn.

rn2kb1r/1bp1pppp/p7/1p1qP3/2pP4/5N2/PP2B.text:
White castles, but our queen and bishop battery is already eyeing the kingside.

Let's continue naturally and open up the dark-squared bishop.

In this line, White has given us everything we wanted.

rn2kb1r/1bp2ppp/p3p3/1p1qP3/2pP4/1P3N2/P.text:
They could try to undermine our structure now, but that's no problem.

We'll just take as there is no point in letting White capture and complicate the position without a reason for it.

rn2kb1r/1bpqpppp/p7/1p1nP1B1/2pP4/2N2N2/.text:
And another move to remember is ...Qd7 in this position.

We unpin the e7-pawn and prepare to play ...e6, develop the bishop to e7 and castle.

A standard and solid kingside plan to combine with our already developed queenside.

rnb1k2r/2p2ppp/pn2p3/1P1qP3/1bpP2Q1/2N2N.text:
White has to either trade the queens and leave us with a more active position, or slide to a square like g4 and target the g7-pawn.

Now this is where you have to know your stuff.

Playing ...Rg8 is simply too passive and gives White the advantage.

We have to take the opportunity to recapture on b5 and offer a trade of rooks here.

rnb1kb1r/2p1pppp/p7/1p1qP3/2pP4/5N2/PP2B.text:
The best they can do right now is develop the bishop to its only available square.

Meanwhile, our bishop will be a monster on b7.

rnbqk2r/2p2ppp/Pn2p3/4P3/1bpP4/2N2N2/1P1.text:
White will continue to capture...

And it's better to trade the rooks here than to take with a minor piece first and leave White's rook active.

rnbqk2r/2p2ppp/p3p3/1P1nP3/1bpP4/2N2N2/1.text:
White could respond with Bd2, defending.

We still managed to develop with tempo, though.

Since we can't recapture on b5, retreating to b6 and protecting the c4-pawn is a good idea.

Another way of protecting the knight on c3 is getting the queen out to c2.

This is a theoretical line that eventually leads to a draw, but it could be dangerous for us.

We still have to deal with the queenside pawns, and we can do that by bringing the knight to b6 and defending c4.

We have to take care, as White probably knows what they are doing if they pick this line.

rnbqk2r/2p2ppp/pn2p3/1P2P3/1bpPQ3/2N2N2/.text:
Centralizing the queen like this isn't a natural move to spot, but it does attack the rook and pose some problems.

Try to think of the most confrontational defense.

And that is bringing the queen to the center ourselves!

The knight is pinned so it can't capture.

rnbqkb1r/1pp1pppp/p4n2/6B1/2pP4/2N2N2/PP.text:
White can choose to activate the bishop to g5 right away. Expect to see this move 15% of the time.

They target our important defender and potentially want to expand in the center next.

But they have let us play ...b5.

We now have a strong queenside pawn chain.

rnbqkb1r/1pp1pppp/p4n2/8/2pPP3/2N2N2/PP3.text:
White could use this opportunity to expand in the center.

Their logic could be that they let us play ...b5, but they want full central control as a compensation.

30% of White players choose to play like this.

We'll accept the challenge and play b5. We're still a pawn up.

rnbqkb1r/2p1pppp/p4n2/1p2P3/2pP4/2N2N2/P.text:
White plays aggressively with e5.

Anything but jumping into the center would be either too dangerous or too passive.

rnbqkb1r/2p1pppp/p4n2/1p4B1/2pP4/2N1PN2/.text:
Since we played ...b5, we now have the b7-square to fianchetto the light-squared bishop, which is an added benefit.

Whether White continues with e3 or e4, we should waste no time but activate the bishop there.

It's already a monster, controlling the center.

rnbqkb1r/2p1pppp/p4n2/1p4B1/2pPP3/2N2N2/.text:
Having achieved ...b5, our plans slightly change against e4 as well.

A forcing move is to develop the bishop and attack the pawn.

Very convenient, indeed.

rnbqkb1r/2p1pppp/p7/1p1NP3/2pP4/5N2/PP3P.text:
Avoiding complications after 7.a4, White could just trade here.

That only activates our queen.

And White can't even attack it.

rnbqkb1r/2p1pppp/p7/1p1nP3/2pP4/2N2N2/PP.text: White developing to e2 basically surrenders and lets us grab control of the position.

rnbqkb1r/2p1pppp/p7/1p1nP3/P1pP4/2N2N2/1.text:
White could choose to play a4 at any point, and combine their central approach with undermining our important pawn chain.

This is definitely a decent move, but I recommend going for ...e6 here.

We are going to develop our light-squared bishop to b7 and avoid blocking it behind a pawn on e6.

rnbqkb1r/2p2ppp/p3p3/1P1nP3/2pP4/2N2N2/1.text:
But doesn't ...e6 sacrifice the pawn on b5?

Well, it opens up the dark-squared bishop!

Suddenly, we are piling up on the pinned knight on c3.

rnbqkb1r/2p2ppp/p3p3/1p1nP3/2pP4/2N2N2/P.text:
We will solidify the knight with ...e6 and simply develop the bishops next, to b7 and e7.

The position effectively plays itself.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/8/2pP4/2N2N2/PP2PP.text:
Once the knight comes out to c3...

We can initiate our idea.

The plan is clear: ...b5.

Let's see some alternative ways of White playing against this approach.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
The Queen's Gambit.

We'll accept it.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/8/2pP4/5N2/PP2PPPP/R.text:
White takes control of the e5-square.

And we'll develop and do likewise with the e4-square.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
In study 3, we will continue to look at the 4.Nc3 lines.

But White doesn't have to play 5.a4 to defend against ...b5.

There are other options that allow us to play it, but rely on activity or central control to counteract our queenside plan.

Let's begin with 1.d4 and our reply of 1...d5.

r2q1rk1/1pp2ppp/p1nbpn2/7b/1P1P4/P1N1PN1.text: They advance the b-pawn, and I suggest an unorthodox-looking move here.

r2q1rk1/pQ1n1ppp/4pn2/1N6/1bBP4/5P2/PP3P.text:
It was important to grab a tempo and check with the bishop rather than just retreat because we now get time to castle.

And once we do that, there are no threats with the knight anymore.

Next, we will kick it out and potentially develop the queen to b6 if we want to trade.

The only thing we should worry about is the open g-file for White, but we are fine.

r2q1rk1/ppp2ppp/2nbpn2/7b/3P4/P1N1PN1P/1.text:
White starts a queenside expansion.

They can't really improve in the center or on the kingside, so a3-b4 is a sound plan.

We'll take away the b5-square.

r2qk2r/pQ1n1ppp/3bpn2/1N6/2BP4/5P2/PP3P1.text:
Once the aforementioned Nb5 arrives...

We can grab a tempo and check on b4!

r2qk2r/pQ1n1ppp/4pn2/1N6/1bBP4/5P2/PP3P1.text:
White can either block with the bishop or move the king.

They will lose castling rights either way.

r2qk2r/pQ1n1ppp/4pn2/2b5/2B5/4PP2/PP3P1P.text:
We can simply recapture with the bishop and our pieces are blossoming.

We are ready to castle, centralize the knight and kick away the White queen with ...Rb8. White also has pawn weaknesses around their king.

We are down a pawn but have a lot  to show for it.

r2qk2r/ppp2ppp/2nbpn2/7b/3P4/2N1PN1P/PP2.text:
Finally, White retreats and unpins.

This is a passive move that works for us.

We will simply castle.

r2qk2r/ppp2ppp/2nbpn2/8/2BP2b1/2N1PN1P/P.text:
So they attack our bishop.

No need to capture right now if there's no added benefit, so we'll just drop it back to h5.

r2qkb1r/pQ1n1ppp/4pn2/2p5/2BP4/2N1PP2/PP.text:
White doesn't have to capture on c5.

They can also choose to go for development and let us capture on d4.

Nc3 also comes in handy for White with potential Nb5 attacks.

We'll capture and make a point of splitting White's pawns.

r2qkb1r/pQ1n1ppp/4pn2/8/2BP4/2N2P2/PP3P1.text:
Now the f-pawns are doubled and isolated, as well as the lone d-pawn.

Now we will be fine as long as we develop naturally.

And the d6-square is best for the bishop right now.

r3qrk1/1pp2ppp/p1nbpn2/7b/1P1P4/P1N1PN1P.text:
It's sliding the queen to e8.

From there, the queen supports our e5-plan and we want to get the rook on the same file as the white queen.

White hasn't done anything inherently wrong and they aren't worse, but this position somehow seems more comfortable for Black from a human standpoint.

rn1qk2r/ppp2ppp/3bpn2/8/2BP2b1/2N1PN2/PP.text:
White activates the knight to c3, and we need to keep an eye out for e4 ideas.

However, the simple ...Nc6 should suffice.

White can't push e4 because we would capture on f3 and potentially on d4.

On the other hand, we should look to push ...e5 once we castle and take advantage of the pin on the knight.

rn1qkb1r/pQ3ppp/4pn2/2p5/2BP4/4PP2/PP3P1.text:
A move to consider is White accepting the pawn on b7.

Our rook is under attack right now, so we don't have much of a choice.

We'll have to move the knight to d7.

rn1qkb1r/pp3ppp/4pn2/2P5/2B5/1Q2PP2/PP3P.text:
If they capture, they've just split their pawns.

We don't have to recapture right away.

rn1qkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/8/2BP2b1/4PN2/PP3P.text:
This does leave the c4-pawn hanging, though, which White will take advantage of.

The material is equal again but White is not going to be pushing e4 anytime soon and we've got natural development to follow.

We'll start with ...e6 to open up the dark-squared bishop. It also prevents any tricks with Bxf7+ and Ne5+.

rn1qkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3bN3/2BP2P1/4PP1P/.text:
And the whole idea was to rotate the bishop to d5.

Now we want to trade for White's active bishop on c4 instead of the knight.

This is a small win for us as White has over-extended and weakened the pawns around their king without getting what they wanted.

rn1qkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/4N3/2BPb1P1/4PP1P/.text: White will most likely weaken their kingside even more.

rn1qkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/7b/2BP2P1/4PN1P/PP.text:
White could be persistent.

This weakening of the kingside is usually compensated by Ne5 to capture our bishop.

But that doesn't have to be the case, as you will see.

We'll retreat to the only possible square.

rn1qkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/8/2BP2b1/1Q2PN2/PP.text:
An aggressive approach is Qb3.

Unpinning the knight, White attacks our b7-pawn.

You shouldn't face this move more than 10% of the time.

Let's take the knight first.

rn1qkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/8/2BP2b1/4PN1P/PP3.text:
White could try to attack our bishop on move 6.

This is played about a quarter of the time.

It's best to retreat.

Capturing on f3 would activate White's queen with an attack on the b7-pawn.

rn1qkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/8/2BP2b1/4PN2/PP3P.text:
The calm and natural approach is simply castling.

Both players will just develop and there won't be many fireworks before the middlegame.

Sometimes it's just like that.

Since White can't play Bg5 and cause trouble, we can comfortably develop our bishop to d6.

rn1qkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/8/2BP4/1Q2PP2/PP3P.text:
White has to recapture and double their pawns.

And this is where an important move comes in.

We don't have to protect the b7-pawn, but instead we'll undermine White's center while activating our pieces.

And that is best done with the gambit ...c5!

rn1qkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pnb1/4N3/2BP2P1/4P2P/P.text:
And once the knight arrives on e5, we don't have to let White trade on their own terms.

We can actually bring the bishop to e4 and attack the rook here.

When there is a pawn on d5 and on c2 this doesn't work, but this is the QGA!

rn2kb1r/ppq2ppp/4pn2/2P5/2B5/1Q2PP2/PP3P.text:
We can defend the b7-pawn now and prepare to capture on c5 with the bishop.

White can't defend the c5-pawn anymore, so we come out on top in this line.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/8/2pP4/4PN2/PP3PPP.text:
Instead, White settles for e3.

For the price of blocking the queen's bishop, they attack c4 immediately, forcing us to make a decision.

The popularity of this move is about 35%.

Instead of the premature ...b5 which runs into a4, I suggest we activate the bishop.

The idea is to get it out and pin the White knight before playing ...e6.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
White goes for the Queen's Gambit.

We'll accept.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/8/2pP4/5N2/PP2PPPP/R.text:
The knight comes out to f3 now.

White prevents us from playing ...e5.

We'll develop and prevent the immediate e4.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
In the final study of the chapter, we will look at an alternative to 4.Nc3.

That is the early e3, which White plays in order to attack the c4-pawn as quickly as possible.

And they can't play e4.

As ever, let's begin with 1.d4 for White and our reply of 1...d5.
